rule: Use the symbolVariant modifier on view hierarchies to apply variants like fill or outline across nested components.
quote: This modifier sets the specified variant in the environment, so it's great to use on a whole view hierarchy, like we're doing here.

rule: Design actions that complete tasks fully without opening the app unless necessary; use follow-up questions instead.
quote: Your action should perform the task completely, and you should avoid opening your app into the foreground, unless it's necessary for your use case. Where possible, you should ask follow-up questions instead of opening the app.

rule: Donate actions to the system so Siri learns usage patterns and suggests them in Suggestions, Search, and Lock screen.
quote: If you donate actions to the system, Siri will automatically learn how people use your app and will suggest your actions at the right time, in the Suggestions widget, in Search, and on the Lock screen.

rule: Use outlined symbols in toolbars, navigation bars, and lists where symbols appear alongside text.
quote: An outlined, or default variant, of a symbol is great for Toolbars, Navigation Bars, Lists and other places in the UI where symbols are presented alongside text or where symbols need to display a uniform appearance.

rule: Use symbols to reduce visual complexity and communicate quickly, as they are largely language-independent.
quote: They are the simplest form of communication between the user and a product and serve as little pieces of a puzzle that aid in usability and intuitive navigation. They also make interfaces faster to use, helping us navigate quickly, as most symbols are language-independent.

rule: Design high-contrast text on dark backgrounds early, as it benefits low-vision users and the general population.
quote: Apple developed this product, and the primary focus was to be able to read the time, and so the contrast with the black background with the legible letters was very important. Well, it turns out that was also important for low-vision users, and it's great for the person who needs that accessibility, but it also turns out to be useful for everyone else.

rule: Provide voice output alongside visual features so blind or low-vision users access content equivalent to sighted users.
quote: When it was introduced, I think it really surprised everybody, especially because it even had some really neat little features like Mickey's tapping his foot, but to a low-vision or blind audience, if I touched the watch, all I would get is a description, or maybe, perhaps, the time spoken by the same text-to-speech I hear everywhere else on the watch face, and that's just not good enough.

rule: Use the theme-color meta tag to align the browser tab bar with your site's design, extending content to window edges.
quote: To provide your choice for the toolbar color, put it in the HTML head using a meta tag with name="theme-color," and use the content attribute to specify the color.

rule: Set separate theme-color values for light and dark modes using media attributes on meta tags.
quote: You can support both Light and Dark Mode by setting two colors. Yes, now you can add media attributes to meta tags. In this case, media="(prefers-color-scheme: light)" in the first meta tag and "(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" in the second.

rule: Put fallback theme-color declarations first, not last, so browsers without media attribute support use the first declaration.
quote: In browsers that do support name="theme-color" but don't yet support using the media attribute on meta tags, those browsers will use the first theme-color declaration and ignore the rest. So put your fallback first, not last, the way you do in CSS.

rule: Prioritize features by importance and make essential ones immediately visible on the main screen.
quote: The essential parts of your app should be immediately visible to people. It's okay for the non-essential parts to require some navigation to reach.

rule: Avoid hamburger menus for primary navigation; use visible alternatives like tab bars so users see available sections.
quote: When we tested our interface in the hands of people and found out that, when the hamburger menu is closed, people don't know what's inside. The three lines don't convey anything about the features inside. So, instead, we decided to go with a tab bar navigation system, which appears at the bottom of an app and lets people quickly switch between different sections.

rule: Limit tab bar buttons to avoid reducing tappable area and increasing visual complexity that obscures features.
quote: What if all the features are equally important, and I have to cram them all into one space with six tab buttons? But too many tabs reduces the tappable area of each tab and increases the complexity of your app, which can make it harder for people to locate information.

rule: Use familiar words and visual symbols to provide recognizable cues that guide people through your interface.
quote: Second, use words and symbols people are familiar with to provide visual cues.

rule: Hint at gestural interactions rather than hiding them entirely, so people discover and learn gestures naturally.
quote: Third, use gestures for fluid navigation, but hint at gestures.

rule: Surface the most useful and timely information people return to your app for, prioritizing personal, informational, and contextual content.
quote: Three useful principles we've found to focus on when thinking about ideas is to look for things that are personal, informational and contextual.

rule: Show glanceable details and key information at a glance without requiring users to open the app to find it.
quote: Glanceable details like the start time and event location save people a potential step in opening the app to find this information.

rule: Adapt widget content based on context and time of day, showing relevant information before users need to search for it.
quote: Context helps surface the right information at the right moment and allows for a better experience that at its best feels like it's magically predicting someone's needs and next steps.

rule: Vertically center symbols with text cap height and weight-match them so they appear consistent despite scaling differences.
quote: When symbols appear next to text they are vertically centered with a cap height, still there are other typography guidelines we need to consider.

rule: Compensate symbol weight when scaling to maintain optical consistency; small scales appear lighter and large scales bolder without adjustment.
quote: Small symbols are approximately 20 percent smaller than the medium scale and large symbols are about 30 percent larger than the medium scale. But as we can see, only scaling the symbol will make them appear to have different weights.

rule: Prioritize user control by allowing people to share approximate location and function without requiring precise location data.
quote: First, when designing for location privacy, prioritize user control. Give everyone control over the location data that they share and respect their preferences.

rule: Use clear writing at critical decision points to explain what data your app requests and what value it provides to users.
quote: Clear language, especially at important decision points, like here on first app launch, explains what data our app asks for and what value it provides.

rule: Show status of shared location data persistently but reduce prominence after initial interaction to balance transparency without distraction.
quote: When people first launch Maps, that status appears larger and stronger in visual treatment. This reminds them of past decisions and gives them direct access to control of the setting. Once people show interest and interact elsewhere in the app, the visual treatment reduces in prominence.

rule: Keep watchOS apps lightweight and limit lengthy interactions; display all essential information at a glance without scrolling.
quote: When designing your Watch app, keep in mind that Watch apps should be lightweight. Like in this example from the Sleep Cycle app, limit lengthy interactions and be choosy when it comes to functionality. Ideally you can get all the information from your Watch app at a glance.

rule: Make secondary actions discoverable and visible directly in the app instead of hiding them in gesture-based contextual menus.
quote: Secondly, relevant actions should always be visible in the app. And thirdly, eliminate gesture-based contextual menus without removing functionality.

rule: Use sort and filter options at the top of lists to help users narrow down long lists and find relevant information in the moment.
quote: A long scrolling list can become much easier to use, and more personal, if you have the ability to sort and filter to just the information relevant to you in the moment.

rule: Integrate your app with system intelligence entry points like Shortcuts, sharing suggestions, and Siri to extend beyond the home screen.
quote: Your app can participate in intelligence by integrating with the system, which allows the system to see your app as much more than a monolithic container.

rule: Question basic assumptions about feature design from the start; convert problems into opportunities.
quote: question assumptions from the start. Ask questions. Ask, "Why are we doing it this way?"

rule: Remove obstacles to getting started; focus on effortless entry to core functionality.
quote: focused on removing obstacles to getting started with each of your drills and workouts

rule: Design shortcuts for frequently repeated, valuable actions that work by voice without visual browsing.
quote: a great use for shortcuts will be something that is valuable, or interesting to repeat. Doable with your voice by not relying on visuals or tapping.

rule: Place Add to Siri buttons selectively near high-intent actions, not on every menu item.
quote: Don't do this, where you put an Add to Siri button on every item on your main menu

rule: Keep shortcut parameter summaries short, verb-first, and exclude app name; show optional parameters under Show More.
quote: Summaries should read like a sentence and start with a verb. There's no need to write the name of your app in the summary

rule: Prefill suggested shortcut invocation phrases with a short, speakable, memorable phrase.
quote: Try to keep this phrase short and descriptive about the kind of action that the user just did. And because the user will be able to say this to Siri, it should also be easy to speak and remember.

rule: Present Add to Siri immediately after the user performs an action they are likely to repeat.
quote: this is a great time to present an Add to Siri button because the user just performed an action that they're very likely to repeat

rule: Design direct, responsive gesture interactions that feel like an extension of the user's mind and body.
quote: when the tool feels like an extension of your mind. An extension of your mind.

rule: Make pointer effects adapt shape to the control type being hovered.
quote: a fluid adaptive pointer that morphs into controls when hovering over them to adapt its accuracy and provide a clear indication that you're about to interact with them

rule: Change pointer shape contextually: beam for text, arrows for drag targets, standard elsewhere.
quote: When hovering over text, for example, the pointer changes into a beam and snaps to lines to make interacting with text easier

rule: Prioritize high-level APIs over low-level for pointer; they offer polished, consistent behavior.
quote: Start with the higher-level APIs. They'll offer you the most polished experience with tuned behaviors and visuals that are consistent with similar UI in the rest of the system

rule: Use sidebar navigation on iPad to show both content and navigation on one screen.
quote: instead of empty space, it fills the display with the content that you want to see, your photos, as well as your navigation controls on the left

rule: Avoid full-screen transitions on iPad; update parts of screen instead to use large display efficiently.
quote: Flatten your app's navigation. Avoid big full-screen transitions in favor of updating part of the screen at a time

rule: Support Auto Layout fully so iPad app layouts adapt to arbitrary Mac window resizing.
quote: By fully supporting Auto Layout in your iPad app, your interface will be resizable on Mac

rule: Make all text dynamic if possible; text that can grow should grow with user's font size setting.
quote: First, you make as much of your text dynamic as possible. If the text can grow, it should grow

rule: Scale glyphs and icons alongside text to maintain visual balance as text size grows.
quote: you should scale glyphs that appear next to text so that your UI continues to look balanced

rule: All apps should support Dark Mode; users expect it when device is set to Dark Mode.
quote: In general, all of your apps should support Dark Mode. When the people using your app have set their device to be in Dark Mode, they'll expect your app to change as well

rule: Design symbols to sit on the same baseline as adjacent text, with invisible margins that ensure proper alignment.
quote: When symbols appear next to text, they all sit nicely on the same baseline.

rule: Present content immediately upon app launch with live, playing material to engage users and reduce friction.
quote: Apple TV has purposefully migrated its designs towards a content first experience. And all that really means is something's on, something's playing. When you launch into the application, it's alive.

rule: Avoid forcing sound and video on launch; allow users to invoke audio after content appears.
quote: it's important to note here that that trailer, we don't force sound on the viewer in this instance. Too much sound and video when you first launch into something, it can be destructive.

rule: Eliminate latency and remove overstimulation by minimizing animations, icons, images, and text styles that compete for attention.
quote: By using too many animations, icons, images and text styles, it competes for somebody's attention. And we don't want somebody be-- to be in that competitive mindset. We want them to be focused and relaxed.

rule: Synchronize haptic feedback with on-screen animations to create causality: make the relationship between user action and sensory response obvious.
quote: Causality is about, for feedback to be useful; it must be obvious what caused it.

rule: Match haptic and audio feedback to the physical properties of what users interact with, as they would expect from real-world objects.
quote: Now, when designing sounds for your experiences, think about what would it feel and sound like, if what you interact with would be a physical object.

rule: Synchronize haptic sensations from the Taptic Engine with audio output to create combined audio-haptic experiences.
quote: The haptic sensations from the taptic engine are synchronized to the sounds coming from the speaker, and the result is what we call an audio haptic experience.

rule: Use continuous haptic experiences for sustained feedback and transient haptics for momentary impacts, strikes, or taps.
quote: So, we can play these continuous experiences. We can also have something that's more shorter and compact. It's a single cycle, and we call this experience a transient. It's much more momentary, and it feels like an impact or a strike or a tap.

rule: Create notification sounds that clearly convey their message without requiring users to look at the screen.
quote: if your app relies on notifications, it makes a lot of sense to think about creating your own notification sound

rule: Design notification sounds to be easily recognizable so users instantly know which app sent them.
quote: This sound is easily recognizable. When you hear this, you know it's coming from Dark Sky.

rule: Use sound to help users understand interactions better and give devices a voice to communicate with them.
quote: It helps us understand interactions better. And it gives our devices a voice so they can tell us things, they can talk back to us.

rule: Answer core design questions before implementation: what are you making, who is it for, and does it work.
quote: Questions like, what are we making? Who is it for? Does it actually work? And did we get it right?

rule: Define your app by identifying features that matter most to users and serve your own goals.
quote: take all the things you can imagine your app could do. Identify the features that matter most to the people who will use your app

rule: Send notifications sparingly and only when urgent or deeply relevant to avoid users disabling them.
quote: Carefully consider how frequently you send notifications to people. They will get annoyed if you send notifications too often.

rule: Use location and time context to determine notification relevance and improve user experience.
quote: The two main contextual factors that are used to determine relevancy are location and time.

rule: Complement apps with Apple Watch notifications that are valuable and useful, not interruptive.
quote: the notifications that you send to people should contain valuable and useful information. People should actually feel thankful for the notifications that you send to them.

rule: Design for performance by optimizing UI graphics and using asynchronous loading on watch apps.
quote: The design of your app's UI and how you produce graphics can have a huge impact on the performance of your app. You want to design for performance.

rule: Remove friction by streamlining the first-time experience to get players into your game as quickly as possible.
quote: making a great first impression and a really frictionless first time experience in the game, really streamlining everything that gets in the way

rule: Load only essential assets to reach the first interactive screen, then load remaining content asynchronously.
quote: Load just enough of your assets so that you can get up and running to your first interactive screen. And then use technologies like Grand Central Dispatch

rule: Prototype before coding to test ideas and avoid building the wrong thing for your users.
quote: instead of going from an idea directly to building your application, we're going to go from an idea to a prototype, and then build our application

rule: Show prototypes to real users and ask if they understand the interaction, find it easy, and how to improve it.
quote: Do you know how to do this one particular thing that we have prototyped? Is it easy to do that thing? And in general, how can we make this better?

rule: Remove UI elements that don't serve the immediate task; let people focus on essential actions.
quote: They remove the UI and allow people to focus on what they need, which is to find something, to ask a question, to get their bearings.

rule: Design apps for the context where they will actually be used, accounting for users' physical and mental state.
quote: They considered the context really well, the context that this will be used in. They took into account where and when people would pull out their phone and launch their app.

rule: Make apps feel simple and natural so users perceive them as an extension of what they already know.
quote: When an app feels simple users perceive it as natural, an extension of what they know. It feels like it arises from their experience and it flows naturally from what they expect.

rule: Design feedback for three interaction phases: before (anticipation), during (response), and after (completion).
quote: We can think of these phases in terms of a physical button. Before I have pressed the button it's just hanging out there. During my interaction with that button it's being pressed in. And finally after I've pressed that button my finger is lifting off of it and it's returning to its original state.

rule: Use both telling (text and icons) and showing (visual, audio, haptic changes) to communicate feedback.
quote: The first is that you can tell people, you can literally put text on screen explaining what's going on or design icons that explain things. The second is that you can show people, you can allow people to experience the results of their action more like the real world through visual, audio or even haptic change over time.

rule: Make notifications beautiful, helpful, actionable, and respectful of people's time and attention.
quote: Thoughtfully designed notifications are a powerful way to communicate timely information to people that they will find valuable and useful. Learn how you can design notifications people want to receive by making them beautiful, helpful, actionable, and respectful of their valuable time and attention.

rule: Offer quiet notifications that go to notification center without lock screen, sound, or haptic interruption.
quote: At the top, the first option is to deliver quietly. And these quiet notifications will be send directly into your notification center without interruption. It did not appear on the lock screen. It did not play a sound or haptic, or present as banners.

rule: Use rich notifications to provide context and information so users understand without launching the app.
quote: Rich notifications are a great way to provide more context and information around each notification. That way you can see one, understand what it's for and get the extra information that you need to take action. And it all happens right in line. You don't need to launch into the app and lose the context of what you're doing.

rule: Clarify your presentation objectives and the bigger picture before diving into details and minutia.
quote: Try not to dive in to details and minutia before you clarify the bigger picture.

rule: Show how you have integrated audience feedback into designs to demonstrate you are listening and responding.
quote: Integrate their feedback. Let them know how it affected your designs. Show that you're listening and responding.

rule: Tag all design assets with the correct color profile to enable accurate color management across devices.
quote: As a designer makes sure to tag your assets properly to allow for color management to accurately display your colors.

rule: Use 16-bit color depth with Display P3 to reduce banding in gradients compared to 8-bit sRGB.
quote: When working with the Display P3 color profile you have the opportunity to also use a larger color depth. 16 bit per channel instead of the usual 8. That allows you to represent more colors within the wide gamut, which is especially useful for gradients.
finding: Display P3 at 16-bit shows much less visible banding than 8-bit sRGB gradients

rule: Work on a wide gamut display when creating Display P3 assets to maintain full control over colors.
quote: Make sure to work on a wide gamut display that supports Display P3 like the MacBook Pro of the Touch Bar, the iMac Retina, or the LG5K Display.

rule: Use PNG format with Save As in Photoshop to embed color profiles and maintain color depth in exported assets.
quote: It is key then to use Save As and PNG as your format because this is the only way at the moment to both imbed a color profile and maintain the color depth without -- in the exported asset.

rule: Design iMessage apps to be playful and personal, allowing users to express themselves in unique and colorful ways.
quote: Using Stickers is playful, and personal. There are so many different types of ways to send Stickers, expressing yourself in unique and colorful ways is fun.

rule: Enable core financial transactions in iMessage without leaving the conversation using Apple Pay.
quote: Apple Pay allows you to perform financial transactions without leaving messages. It is super convenient.

rule: Design collaborative apps in iMessage to require and enable participation from both parties to create engagement.
quote: Games and polling rely on both parties to participate, to make the most of the app experience.

rule: Make alert titles and actions understandable without reading message details; design so users grasp the situation at a glance.
quote: If people scan the title and the actions, ideally, they should be able to understand what is going on without paying too much attention to the message details.

rule: Structure alerts to answer three questions: what happened, why users see this, and how to proceed based on the information.
quote: A good alert answers three key questions. What happened? Why people are seeing this? And how this should proceed based on the information they've received.

rule: Design interfaces to be intuitive and self-explanatory; minimize or eliminate upfront instruction and onboarding tutorials.
quote: You should strive to design your interfaces to be as intuitive and as easy to understand as possible. Ideally no upfront instruction is needed at all.

rule: Limit text styles to two or three per screen to create clear hierarchy while maintaining visual consistency.
quote: In most cases, we recommend using two to three of these text styles per screen.

rule: Design glyphs with high simplification, conceptual universality, and quick readability to communicate function or purpose clearly.
quote: Effective glyphs have some key characteristics. They're highly simplified in form. They're conceptually universal, and they're quickly readable in context as to their function or purpose.

rule: Use optical balance and scaling to adjust glyphs of different shapes, accounting for surface area differences to appear equal in visual weight.
quote: Because the elliptical shape of messages and the narrow shape of phone have less surface area, we can use scale to achieve this optical balance.

rule: Keep app icons simple and clear with no clutter; design for quick, easy recognition at multiple sizes.
quote: The second, simplicity; your design should be simple and clear, no clutter or over complicate it. If your icon is designed well, it should be quick and easy to read.

rule: Maintain icon lineage across versions; refine identity deliberately over time rather than changing icons with each app update.
quote: And lineage, make changes to your icon meaningful and deliberate. Don't change your app icon every single time that you update your app. Refine your identity over time.

rule: Ensure visual consistency across platforms by using the same metaphor and design in both iOS and Mac versions of an app.
quote: The visual connection here is really important because it tells users that they can expect at consistent experience across platforms.

rule: Design interfaces to provide safety, predictability, clarity, achievement, and beauty to meet users' fundamental human needs.
quote: We have the need for safety and predictability. We have a need for knowledge, for meaning, and understanding. We have a need to accomplish tasks, to achieve our personal and professional goals. And we have the need to experience beauty and joy.

rule: Use design principles as foundations for decisions, not just techniques; they express universal truths about perception and behavior.
quote: Design principles don't tell us how to do specific things in our design, they tell us why we should do those things. They serve as the foundation upon which great designs are built.

rule: Help users understand content and locate key information by using clear headings and titles.
quote: Help your users orient themselves with headings and titles. Make sure that the important information from your instructions is conveyed and that commonly used terms are clear.

rule: Provide context clues for informal language so users can understand meaning even if unfamiliar.
quote: If you do, do a quick check to make sure that it's not offensive and be sure to offer contextual clues so that even if a user isn't totally sure what you mean they can still figure it out.

rule: Use simple glyphs and silhouettes in icons rather than detailed depictions to avoid excluding users.
quote: When depicting people keep in mind that more detailed icons may exclude some of your users, but that simpler glyphs like this silhouette are much more general and maybe a better choice.

rule: Send notifications only when your app has important information, never to boost traffic or engagement.
quote: We should send notifications only when they're relevant. Don't spam. Don't send them to boost traffic or engagement, but only when your app has some important information to share.

rule: Make notifications self-contained packages of information allowing users to complete specific tasks without launching the app.
quote: Don't think of notifications as just a hook into your app. You know, they should be a self-contained package of information that allows you to complete a specific task.

rule: Provide contextually relevant additional information in the expanded view of a notification.
quote: And here is where you should provide some additional context, some additional information around your notification.

rule: Test interactive prototypes in realistic contexts on the target device, not in abstract settings.
quote: It is also very important to show your prototypes in context, on the device they're meant for, in a somewhat realistic situation. You can't test things in a vacuum.

rule: Design the first screen to immerse players in the game style before showing functional text or requirements.
quote: No matter what you need to say first, whether it is Accept Terms, or Headsets Recommended, design the first screen to fit within the style of your game. That way, they're immersed immediately.

rule: Entertain or educate during loading to make wait times feel shorter and more valuable.
quote: During Loading, make it fun by educating or entertaining; then, Loading won't see to take as long.

rule: Show progress bars instead of activity indicators to communicate what is happening and how long it will take.
quote: Always favor progress bars over activity indicators because they do a much better job communicating what's happening and how long it will take.

rule: Make the main call to action most dominant in your menu UI, especially in busy interfaces with news and stores.
quote: Make sure that the main call to action to play, start, battle, or begin a new game is the most dominant in your Main Menu UI.

rule: Place controls in consistent, predictable locations throughout your game interface to improve usability.
quote: Consistency improves usability because it helps people mentally map your interface. It's much easier to play and navigate when controls are in predictable locations.

rule: Include three visual states for all buttons and controls: normal, pressed, and disabled to prevent confusion.
quote: In your interface, for clarity, it's important always to include three visual states for buttons and controls because a lack of visual feedback can confuse players. Be sure to use a Normal state to show people that something's tappable. Use a Press state when something has been tapped. And finally, use a Disabled state for control that's not currently active or enabled.

rule: Use disabled state rather than hiding controls, so players understand location and future availability.
quote: Many developers struggle if they should remove or hide a control if it cannot be activated, but if you do that, when it does pop back it could be really confusing to players, especially if this happens during gameplay. So, for a much better user experience, use a Disabled state. This lets people know the control's location and action that will be possible

rule: Establish shared terminology with your team and clients to eliminate confusion and build credibility.
quote: Using the same terminology. This saves time, eliminates confusion, and increases credibility with your team and clients.

rule: Create a single source of truth for approved design deliverables accessible to the entire team.
quote: What if you and your team or client could agree before hand a single place where all of the approved deliverables can be accessed. This would ensure that everyone knows where to go to check out the necessary assets.

rule: Show prototypes and implementations to stakeholders rather than explaining designs with static mockups.
quote: Show and tell. Or rather show more than tell. Designers can be guilty of throwing static mockups inspects over to engineers, especially in a time crunch.

rule: Design learning materials with explicit cognitive models about how people absorb knowledge, not passive transmission.
quote: lectures, as a medium, have no carefully-considered cognitive model at their foundation

rule: Shoulder metacognitive burden (feedback loops, task planning, progress monitoring) for users so they focus on content, not self-regulation.
quote: courses handle much of this metacognitive burden. Their syllabi offer a scheduled scope and sequence, so students need do less planning of their own

rule: Build hierarchy with order, spacing, and contrast to guide attention to the most important item on screen.
quote: Clarity is built with hierarchy, using order, spacing, and contrast to guide people to what's most important. When your hierarchy is strong, the most important item on the screen is always the most obvious one.

rule: Use plain language; strip jargon and speak naturally to reduce friction and respect people's time.
quote: Concise interfaces use plain language. They strip away jargon and speak naturally. They avoid redundancy and get straight to the point.

rule: Guarantee sufficient text contrast by separating color levels by at least five steps for small text and four for icons and large text.
quote: Any two colors are guaranteed to have sufficient contrast for small text if they are at least five levels apart, and at least four levels apart for icons and large text.

rule: Design interfaces to guide users toward intent rather than exposing visible menus and forms.
quote: the web is evolving beyond menus, forms, and endless clicks toward experiences shaped around human intent

rule: Separate interface markup from art direction by architecting the system to serve intentional motion design.
quote: the architecture must serve the art direction

rule: Maintain absolute control over motion by using distance-based math and event-driven animation libraries.
quote: distance-based math to maintain absolute control over their designers' intentional motion

rule: Use real-time collaboration and cursor feedback to encourage active participation in group design work.
quote: Teachers can facilitate collaborative group learning while encouraging active participation from students

rule: Provide code generation and design-to-code mapping to teach students how design concepts translate to implementation.
quote: Dev Mode is great for learning how design concepts map to code concepts

rule: Use familiar layouts and patterns to capture attention and prepare the brain for familiar cognitive states.
quote: I'm usually super attentive when looking at my notes. This ad puts my brain in that same state of mind as soon as it recognizes the layout.

rule: Create unexpectedness by breaking context: place dissimilar elements among similar ones to be remembered.
quote: When multiple similar objects are present, the one that differs from the rest is most likely to be remembered.

rule: Let users customize text size, colors, fonts, and layout density so they can tailor the interface to their individual needs.
quote: you can adjust the text size, change the colors, choose 'high-legibility' characters in the San Francisco font, or choose a different font all together

rule: Adopt accessibility APIs like VoiceOver, Switch Control, and Voice Control so assistive technology users can operate your app.
quote: adopt the Accessibility APIs so that people who use accessibility features can also use your app. Adopting Accessibility APIs will help you close the rest of the inclusion gap

rule: Identify and track inclusion gaps—where user abilities don't match environmental design—as technical debt to close iteratively.
quote: Think of this as inclusion tech debt, or just inclusion debt for short. This is normal. Inclusion is a journey, it's not a one-time thing

rule: Use optical sizes for fonts: smaller text needs wider letter-spacing and sturdier thin strokes for legibility.
quote: When type becomes smaller, letters tend to need more space between them, so that they eye can more easily tell them apart.

rule: Apply tracking (letter-spacing) consistently with optical size changes to prevent abrupt spacing shifts at size transitions.
quote: With no tracking, the difference in native spacing between SF Text and Display would have been an issue when we switched from one font to the other at 20 points.

rule: Use the tracking API instead of kerning to tighten truncated strings and preserve ligatures for consistent word rhythm.
quote: with a kerning API, that ligature remains and breaks the rhythm of the word. On the other hand, with the tracking API, we take of de-assembling that ligature for you

rule: Place primary content in the center of the field of view and spread secondary content horizontally to match landscape perception.
quote: It's easiest to see things in the center, so place the most important content there. And the field of view is wide, so use landscape layouts.

rule: Fade content in and out during large movements in immersive experiences to prevent disorientation and maintain user comfort.
quote: avoid large, fast movement. This could feel disorienting. Instead, we recommend fading out content while it's in motion and fading it back in once it's settled.

rule: Build extreme versions of features—fastest and safest—then converge toward a balanced solution.
quote: What's the fastest version we could do? What's the safest? This approach helps you explore different extremes and forces you to break out of the usual boundaries. Build both extremes, test them internally, and then converge toward a balanced solution that works.

rule: Ensure designs remain readable when magnified; test proximity of information at magnified zoom levels.
quote: Consider how the relative proximity of information changes when a page is magnified.

rule: Provide captions and transcripts for all videos and animations containing meaningful audio.
quote: Transcribe and caption all videos and animations that have meaningful audio.

rule: Avoid complex language, autoplaying animations, and flashing content to reduce cognitive load.
quote: Designers should avoid complex language, autoplaying animations and videos, and flashing animations.

rule: Design keyboard-first navigation; test that pages read logically to screen reader users.
quote: Follow keyboard guidelines and test with a screen reader to ensure the page is read to the user in a logical order.

rule: Map touch gestures naturally to actions; make gestures smooth and immediately responsive.
quote: The gestures are smooth, quick to pick up, and immediately responsive.

rule: Show resolution or completion of time-sensitive alerts; closure reinforces habit of engagement.
quote: Communicating the happy resolution of an Amber Alert would show people that they can really make a difference. Especially since 95% of Amber Alerts are resolved within the first 48 hours.
finding: 95% of Amber Alerts resolved within 48 hours

rule: Make initial actions require minimal effort to encourage immediate engagement.
quote: People are more likely to take action when the effort is small.

rule: Show work on lengthy processes; users value outcomes more when they see the underlying effort.
quote: People trust and value things more when they see the underlying work.

rule: Avoid pre-selected options and fear-based language in upsells; they erode trust long-term.
quote: fear-based tactics will never work long-term

rule: Provide contextual guidance and help at the moment of need, not lengthy upfront explanations.
quote: Rather than asking your users to remember everything up-front, you should provide guidance as they go.

rule: Use loss framing ethically when it clearly benefits the user, not merely the business.
quote: Loss framing is ethical here because it clearly benefits the user (prevents getting locked out), not just Google.

rule: Show the number of existing users or adoption to reduce social uncertainty about new products.
quote: Showing off the number of people who are already using it.

rule: Show only core differentiators when warning of feature loss, not exhaustive lists that increase cognitive load.
quote: focusing only on the core differentiators would be a lot more impactful

rule: Detect usage decline and proactively suggest new feature uses before users initiate cancellation.
quote: Start introducing new ways of using your product when you detect a decline in usage

rule: Avoid mandatory surveys in offboarding flows; they trigger reactance and yield low-quality data.
quote: mandatory but unnecessary steps block a natural flow, it creates reactance

rule: Provide specific feature requirements and stylistic guidance in prompts; avoid vague requests that lead to arbitrary layouts.
quote: your prompts need to be much more specific. Take some time to think through the features and high-level points you want the app to have from the get-go.

rule: Build tuning panels alongside animations to shorten feedback loops and adjust parameters in real time without context switching.
quote: make a tuning panel, shorten the feedback loop, and get to what feels optimal for your app.

rule: Populate prototypes with realistic edge cases: empty states, long text, unbounded lists, and variable-length content.
quote: stop and think through edge cases yourself. For example, in my app, how does the detail area look if no meeting has been scheduled yet?

rule: Use ::selectedcontent pseudo-element to display rich content (icons, images) in select buttons, not just text.
quote: use the new element inside it to mirror the rich content of the currently selected option

rule: Apply appearance: base-select to customize select menus with CSS while preserving semantic HTML and accessibility.
quote: Apply `appearance: base-select` to opt into the new styling model, then customize the button with familiar CSS

rule: Place primary search in iOS bottom toolbar for ergonomic reachability; field animates up over keyboard.
quote: When search is placed in the bottom Toolbar, the field elegantly animates up over keyboard, optimizing for reachability, and keyboard input.

rule: Show recent searches inline when search field gains focus; let users remove individual or all searches.
quote: Displaying recent searches, can help people get back to a previous result, without the need to even start typing.

rule: Display predictive suggestions that naturally complete the user's query; visually distinguish user input from completion.
quote: visually distinguish between user input, and the predictive part of the suggestion.

rule: Use scope bar for lightweight filtering across locations or categories; show filters contextual to the query.
quote: For lightweight filtering, Apple provides a control called a scope bar.

rule: Display a no-results view with search icon, title, and subtitle; show the search text to help catch typos.
quote: display a well-considered empty state, or no results view. A completely blank view can leave someone wondering if their search even went through.

rule: Prioritize clarity and trust over brand expression in financial or critical contexts.
quote: Clarity and trust come first here, not brand expression. Balance belongs in this app, sets exactly the right expectation, and travels without friction.

rule: Use verbs for features users control; nouns for attributes they observe.
quote: For a feature like this, a verb works well because we're putting the person using it in control. The feature is something you do, not something you have.

rule: Use visibilityPriority modifier to keep critical toolbar actions visible when space is limited.
quote: I want the system to know that it's important to keep them visible. I can do this by adding the new visibilityPriority modifier, and setting the priority to high. Now, the Undo and Redo buttons become visible!

rule: Use toolbarMinimizeBehavior set to onScrollDown to auto-hide navigation bars during scrolling.
quote: So I add the new toolbarMinimizeBehavior modifier, and set it to "onScrollDown" for the navigationBar placement. Now, the system automatically moves the navigation bar out of the way when I scroll.

rule: Design icons with simple, elegant geometry rather than complex fine details to adapt across all sizes and visual conditions.
quote: think in terms of, you know, simple and elegant geometries, not in terms of complex fine details, because those are going to be hard to adapt

rule: Export icon layers at full canvas size to preserve geometry and relative positioning when importing into Icon Composer.
quote: if you export them at the full canvas size, then when you bring them into Icon Composer, they'll all already be correctly positioned

rule: Test icons at their smallest display size and in realistic contexts like home screen groups before finalizing.
quote: put it into a group on your home screen because that's going to be the smallest, it's going to possibly be on your iPhone screen

rule: Use vectors (SVG) instead of bitmaps for app icons to enable scaling across all sizes and visual treatments.
quote: the recommendation is to use scalable vectors, SVG, for which you import

rule: Position controls on the side edge of folding device displays to maximize vertical space for content.
quote: controls that normally sit at the top and bottom move to the right side of the display in order to maximize vertical space

rule: Preserve all controls and functionality across every device pose rather than tying features to specific fold states.
quote: You don't want to tie functionality to a specific pose. So controls move to the side for most of those layouts.

rule: Offset content from the right edge when controls occupy vertical space to prevent blocking interactive elements.
quote: on iPhone Duo, most content needs an offset so it isn't hidden behind the controls

rule: Use displacement patterns to move elements away from the fold while preserving their visual relationships and contextual meaning.
quote: displacement, which adjusts the frame of the existing elements based on the available space, keeping important content visible, reachable, and unobstructed

rule: Avoid displacing continuous scrolling content like articles and feeds; let scrolling handle fold adaptation naturally.
quote: Continuous scrolling content like articles, feeds, documents, and lists don't displace

rule: Surface the user's specific pain point, not exhaustive feature tables, in checkout flows.
quote: Focus the journey of your customers around their most pressing pain point (my Task limit in this case).

rule: Add reassuring feedback at checkout completion to confirm the action resolved the user's constraint.
quote: Have the end of your checkout experience reassure them with a clear feedback loop to minimize frustrations.

rule: Use TimelineView to pass elapsed time to shaders so animation depends only on current parameters, not state.
quote: Shaders are stateless. They have no memory of the previous frame, the output relies only on the parameters. So, if I want animation, I need to pass in a value that changes over time.

rule: Override alignment guides semantically to position views without manual offset calculations.
quote: use alignmentGuide to override an alignment semantically — moving the subview's bottom guide to its top edge so it floats neatly outside its container.

rule: Use event-driven Script Graphs to prototype interactive logic without writing code.
quote: A Script Graph lets me build games through Event Driven logic.

rule: Expose numerical parameters as public input variables so you can iterate while testing on device.
quote: Since I set dragSpeed to be a public variable, it shows up in my Nut's Scripting Component. Which means that I can, while testing it all on my Vision Pro, adjust my dragSpeed to find just the right value.

rule: Compose complex node graphs into reusable Prototyped Subgraphs to keep logic streamlined and shareable.
quote: Building reusable pieces of logic like this allows me to speed up my workflow and keep my logic streamlined.

rule: Use variable overrides per component instance to vary behaviour while sharing the same script logic.
quote: Overrides are unique variations of a variable that are unique to each Scripting Component. This means I can have multiple Nuts in my scene and, while they share the same Script Graph logic, can use different dragSpeed settings.

rule: Scale PDF graphics automatically across watch sizes using 2x scale factor and Automatic property; this reduces file production effort.
quote: prepare your graphics with a scale factor of 2 and save them as PDFs, you can create a single file for usage across all four watch sizes
finding: Scales down 9% for 38mm, up 10% for 44mm with one source file.

rule: Set Digital Crown haptic feedback to align UI events with tactile detents so users perceive consistent interaction feedback.
quote: if your app coordinates events in the UI with Digital Crown rotation, you'll want to make sure that those UI events line up with these new haptic effects

rule: Use Dynamic Type default categories matching watch case size: Small for 38mm, Large for 40–42mm, XLarge for 44mm.
quote: different default content categories that correspond to the watch case size. Small is the default category for 38mm, Large for 40mm and 42mm, and XLarge for 44mm

rule: Present subscription offers immediately when users attempt to access a gated feature, not as a pop-up ad.
quote: present your subscription when a person has shown interest in a feature or piece of content that you offer through your subscription

rule: Limit subscription signup flow to three clicks maximum to achieve 61% conversion; nine clicks drops conversion to 7%.
quote: A subscription flow with three clicks led to a 61 percent conversion rate, and a subscription flow with four clicks led to a 48 percent conversion rate. However, nine clicks... the conversation rate drops significantly to seven percent
finding: 3 clicks = 61% conversion; 4 clicks = 48%; 9 clicks = 7%.

rule: Ask for signup before requesting personalization, favoriting, or additional personal details in subscription flows.
quote: Focus people on singing up first. Personalization, favoriting, and requesting additional personal details can all wait until after someone has signed up

rule: Use Safe Area layout guide to inset content from iPhone X sensor housing, rounded corners, and home indicator in both orientations.
quote: The Safe Area layout guide helps avoid underlapping system UI elements when positioning content and controls

rule: Prefer symbol-only items in vertical bars to conserve space; provide both icon and title in your code so the system can choose the right representation.
quote: Typically, your app specifies two pieces of data on your toolbar content, an icon and a title. Depending on the context and what's specified on the item, the system then chooses what representation to show.

rule: Use axisBehavior API to keep related items on the same axis; set horizontalOnly for items that transition between symbol and text, verticalPreferred for custom views that support vertical layout.
quote: Related items should stay on the same axis. One common instance is an item that transitions between a symbol and a text, like this edit button in Clock. That item shouldn't be placed in a vertical bar, even though the symbol could theoretically be displayed vertically.

rule: Craft button shapes to harmonize with the device's curved display; derive pinned button shapes from the hardware curvature rather than using simple pill shapes.
quote: I'll do that again. The change is subtle, but deriving the shape of the button from the shape of the display itself makes it so that these buttons that are pinned to the bottom of the screen and will harmonize with the hardware of the watch.

rule: Avoid absolute content offset and size values in lazy stacks; they are estimated and unstable during scrolling.
quote: avoid using the absolute content size or content offset with lazy stacks, since these are estimated and unstable

rule: Filter data at the source level, not in view bodies, to keep lazy stack subview counts predictable.
quote: filter at the data level. If you're using SwiftData, use a Predicate to filter your Query

rule: Do not change view layouts after they appear on screen in lazy stacks; use custom layouts instead.
quote: don't change the layout of subviews of lazy stacks after they appear

rule: Use relative scroll position based on visible subviews, not absolute content offset, for visibility checks.
quote: it's better to use the relative positions of subviews in the visible region of the scroll view

rule: Size nested lazy stacks (LazyHStack in LazyVStack) with fixed heights to prevent content cutoff.
quote: fix the view heights. For example, for text, you can set a line limit, and reserve space for shorter text

rule: Move brand color from UI controls into the content area so controls remain unobtrusive with Liquid Glass.
quote: move color into the content area of your app, into the scroll view. That way, Liquid Glass controls sit above the content layer and pick up your brand color dynamically

rule: Use color sparingly to indicate status, feedback, and selection states; avoid overwhelming interfaces.
quote: color can be distracting and make an interface feel overwhelming. Aim to use color in ways that create meaning such as portraying hierarchy, groupings, or indicating interaction

rule: Reserve custom components for high-impact content; use standard components for functional tasks.
quote: Custom components take refinement. So you should focus your time building them for areas of your app that have the biggest impact or make your content stand out. Then, audit your app for opportunities to use standard components for aspects of your app that are functional

rule: Platform conventions for icons differ across iOS, Android, and Web; match platform patterns while maintaining brand.
quote: Even though they've created their own style of icons each of these actions stays true to the platform pattern of sharing

rule: Plan immersive environments in layered depth: background to foreground, to simplify production and asset creation.
quote: visualize your environment in terms of layers, building from the background to the foreground. Identify which scene elements will need to have motion, and start thinking about what spatial audio you can attach to them

rule: Viewers in visionOS see approximately 81° of immersive content in their field of view; compose scenes accordingly.
quote: viewers will see approximately 81° of the scene in their field of view, when fully immersed
finding: 81 degrees field of view

rule: Capture immersive environment photography at 14,400 by 7,200 pixels minimum for sharp output at 40 pixels per degree.
quote: For visionOS, an environment will be sharp at 40 pixels per degree, so 360° panorama of 14,400 by 7,200 pixels is an ideal target
finding: 40 pixels per degree target resolution

rule: Use tripod-leveled primary photography at 1 meter height and secondary camera at 2 meters to fill composition gaps.
quote: use a tripod with your camera leveled 1 meter off the ground, and ensure a deep depth of field. If possible, set up another camera 2 meters off the ground to trigger at the same time. This alternate view is especially helpful during Post-Production, to fill in parts of the scene that are not visible from the primary view

rule: Capture bracketed exposures to preserve detail across lighting range from sun to shadow in immersive environments.
quote: shoot bracketed exposures to ensure you capture all the details

rule: Reduce expensive real-time rendering in immersive environments by layering textures and using precomputed data textures.
quote: Offloading complex shading work to precomputed data textures, allows you to produce motion that would otherwise be too expensive to render real-time

rule: Stack low and high frequency motion patterns to create believable variety without repetition in immersive scenes.
quote: By stacking low frequency and high frequency motion, you can create variety that is never repetitive

rule: Instruct the on-device model to handle negative or harmful user input in an empathetic and constructive way.
quote: I'm appending a sentence to tell the model to respond to negative prompts in an empathetic and wholesome way.

rule: Collect prompts covering all major use cases and safety-triggering scenarios, then automate end-to-end testing or use another LLM to grade responses at scale.
quote: Remember to collect prompts to cover all major use cases of your app, and you will also need to collect prompts that may trigger safety issues.

rule: When a safety error occurs in a user-initiated feature, provide UI feedback explaining the app cannot process the request and offer alternative actions.
quote: For a user-initiative feature, especially one that has someone wait, remember to provide appropriate UI feedback to explain that the app cannot process the request. It can be a simple alert, or you can use this opportunity to provide alternative actions for people to choose from.

rule: Use less than five examples when prompting on-device LLMs; write them directly into the prompt without external references.
quote: You can boost your task performance by giving the model less than five examples of the kinds of outputs you want, and just write those directly into your prompt.

rule: Place the benefit or reason first in instructional copy, then the required action, to maximize message impact and clarity.
quote: Effective messaging in apps, such as error messages, push notifications, and instructional copy, is most effective when you clearly state the benefit first, followed by the action required.

rule: Maintain a word list documenting approved terms, avoided synonyms, and definitions to ensure consistent language across the app.
quote: A word list serves as a reference, ensuring use of the same terms throughout an app. This improves people's understanding of the app. Your word list should include approved words, along with synonyms or alternatives to avoid. Add definitions for clarity.

rule: Reduce immersion automatically during high-motion video playback to prevent viewer discomfort.
quote: Playback will automatically reduce immersion when high motion is detected, which can be more comfortable for the viewer during high motion scenes.

rule: Blur window edges for spatial video to prevent stereo discomfort from unequal object clipping between eyes.
quote: We inset that flat screen behind a window and blur the edges of the window to soften them. This helps avoid issues when an object is clipped by the window more in one eye than the other, which can be uncomfortable to view.

rule: Use billboards for objects beyond 1 kilometer distance where depth perception flattens naturally.
quote: Depth cues start to flatten out from 1 to 3 kilometers. So you can reduce these areas to a flat image without much perceivable loss of depth.

rule: Keep snippet height under 340 points to avoid scrolling and maintain glanceability.
quote: Avoid including content past 340 points in height, which will require scrolling and introduce unexpected friction.

rule: Design snippets to be understood visually without relying on spoken dialog for accessibility.
quote: Challenge yourself to make your snippet understandable on its own, even if the dialog isn't shown or heard. The snippet should clearly communicate the purpose of the intent without relying on dialog.

rule: Remove background customization from navigation and toolbars to preserve automatic glass appearance.
quote: Remove any background customization from your navigation and toolbars. Using UIBarAppearance or backgroundColor interferes with the glass appearance.

rule: Limit Liquid Glass to the most important, interactive elements that users touch directly.
quote: Limit Liquid Glass to the most important elements of your app. Where possible, use the system views and controls for the best experience.

rule: Prevent glass elements from overlapping other glass elements to maintain the illusion of a single floating control layer.
quote: This prevents glass elements from overlapping other glass elements, and keeps the illusion of a single floating layer of glass intact.

rule: Use containerRelative corner configuration so glass corners automatically adapt to their container's corners.
quote: To have corners automatically adapt to their container, use .containerRelative cornerConfiguration. When moving the view closer to the container's corner, its corner radius adapts automatically.

rule: Larger glass sizes render more opaque; smaller sizes render clearer and adapt to light or dark mode automatically.
quote: Glass adapts the appearance based on its size. A larger size is more opaque. A smaller size is clearer, and switches between light and dark mode automatically, to increase contrast.

rule: Set isInteractive to true on glass effects for custom views that need button-like scaling and bouncing feedback.
quote: To get that same kind of interactivity in your custom views, set isInteractive to true on the glassEffect.

rule: Place a minimum of two guide points—one start and one end—along each draw path to enable Draw animations.
quote: At a minimum, a path must contain two guide points to properly compute its draw path. A start point, indicated by an open circle, and an end point, indicated by a closed circle.

rule: Design symbol draw directions intentionally: left-to-right for motion, right-to-left for Arabic, center for symmetry.
quote: For example, wind draws left to right to convey motion, whereas this Arabic character draws from right to left, matching its writing direction. Additionally, some symbols can draw from their center, like this symmetrical symbol.

rule: Remove custom backgrounds from sheets to let the new Liquid Glass material display properly.
quote: If you've used the presentationBackground modifier to apply a custom background to your sheets, consider removing that and let the new material shine.

rule: Use glassEffectContainer to group multiple glass elements so they share a consistent sampling region.
quote: Using a glass container allows these elements to share their sampling region, providing a consistent visual result.

rule: Use concentric rectangle shapes to maintain corner alignment between views and their containers across different displays.
quote: To build views that automatically maintain concentricity with their container, use the concentric rectangle shape. Pass the containerConcentric configuration to the corner parameter of a rectangle and the shape will automatically match its container across different displays and window shapes.

rule: Use monochrome icon rendering in toolbars to reduce visual noise and emphasize app content.
quote: Icons use monochrome rendering in more places, including in toolbars. The monochrome palette reduces visual noise, emphasizes your app's content, and maintains legibility.

rule: Convert text to outlines before exporting SVG layers for icons, since SVG format does not preserve font information.
quote: If I was to use any text too, since the SVG format doesn't preserve fonts, it will need converting to outlines before exporting.

rule: Use four or fewer groups (containing up to four layers each) per icon to maintain visual complexity within optimal bounds.
quote: We found this number provides the right bounds for how much visual complexity an icon should have.
finding: up to 4 groups per icon

rule: Set at least one mono-mode icon element to white and map other colors to gray tones to maximize legibility in monochrome.
quote: Setting at least one element of your icon to be white, usually the most prominent or recognizable part, make sure it shows up strong.

rule: Keep source icon artwork flat, opaque, and simple; add dynamic effects like blur and shadow only in Icon Composer, not the source file.
quote: it's best for me to still my source art down to its graphic essence, so that it's flat, opaque, and easy to control later.

rule: Make RealityKit AnimationPlaybackController observable in SwiftUI to allow real-time UI updates of animation playback state and scrubbing.
quote: In visionOS 26, the existing RealityKit class `AnimationPlaybackController` is now Observable.

rule: Use realityViewLayoutBehavior modifier with fixedSize to make RealityView tightly wrap 3D model bounds like Model3D does by default.
quote: I apply the new `.realityViewLayoutBehavior` modifier with `.fixedSize` to make the RealityView tightly wrap the model's initial bounds.

rule: Add both InputTargetComponent and CollisionComponent to gesture targets in RealityKit to ensure the interaction system recognizes entity gestures.
quote: Pro tip: on any entity that's the target of a gesture, also add both InputTargetComponent and CollisionComponent.

rule: Use frontal, flat perspectives and avoid realistic 3D objects in icon designs, as they compete with material glass effects rather than complement them.
quote: Realistic 3D objects and perspectives like in the previous Chess icon can compete with the material qualities. The redesigned icon uses a frontal view and a more flat appearance.

rule: Show only essential upfront; reveal additional content when people interact, not before.
quote: progressive disclosure. It's about showing only what's necessary upfront — just enough to help people get started then revealing more as they interact

rule: Use lists over grids for structured information; lists take less vertical space and scan faster.
quote: A List works way better, it's a flexible, highly usable and familiar way to show structured information and facilitates quick scanning. It also takes up less vertical space than images

rule: Add gradient or blur behind text on images to improve readability without disrupting design.
quote: One simple way to fix this is by adding a subtle background behind the text like a gradient or blur. It improves readability, while adding some dimension

rule: Use ramp animations (slow ease-in then spring) when views expand to show more content.
quote: It starts with a slow ease-in, then pops to completion with a quick spring. This animation curve tends to work best when views expand to show more content

rule: Show hover effects only from visible elements; hidden content surprises users if revealed accidentally.
quote: hover effects should always start from a visible element. If there's no hint about where something is, it'll be hard to find or surprising if people accidentally discover it

rule: Make scroll views full-width or full-height with clear boundaries so people know where to look to scroll.
quote: your scroll views with Look to Scroll enabled should be the full width or full height of your window. This gives people generous space to scroll and provides clear edges to look at

rule: Create new windows for each document in multitasking apps; do not replace previous context in one window.
quote: When multitasking is enabled, your app should open each document in their own window. This additive behavior is more helpful because windows persist until closed

rule: Provide descriptive, unique names for each open window so users can locate them in the app menu.
quote: Name each window with a unique string, like the title of the document. If your app provides a descriptive name for each window, it will be much easier to find a specific window

rule: Use SwiftUI Animation types to animate UIKit views instead of computing initial velocity manually.
quote: SwiftUI animations already have the ability to preserve velocity at the end of a gesture by merging together during the gesture

rule: Reset transition state by viewDidAppear or viewDidDisappear, which are guaranteed to be called at transition end.
quote: reset it by viewDidAppear or viewDidDisappear. These are guaranteed to be called at the end of the transition

rule: Anchor game UI sections to specific screen sides rather than scaling uniformly to fit different aspect ratios.
quote: break your UI layout into separate sections. Each of which is anchored to a specific side of the screen. As you move between device shapes, you can keep each section at a consistent size

rule: Avoid fear-based language in upsells; fear tactics damage trust and user retention long-term.
quote: fear-based tactics will never work long-term.

rule: Use loading time to add value and help users transition, not just show a spinner.
quote: Why not use those 'loading times' to add value to users? What can you give them to help transition from wherever they were before?

rule: Delay permission and preference requests until after delivering initial value to users.
quote: If you want to ask for information or permissions, make sure you've given value before.

rule: Use visual portraits and object images to make alerts scannable; faces are processed 1,000x better than text descriptions.
quote: your brain processes faces 1,000x better than objects
finding: Face recognition is 1000x faster than object recognition

rule: Show clear resolution or completion of time-sensitive alerts to reinforce positive habit formation and increase future engagement.
quote: Communicating the happy resolution of an Amber Alert would show people that they can really make a difference
finding: 95% of Amber Alerts are resolved within 48 hours; closure creates positive association reinforcing habit

rule: Avoid misleading framing that disguises or conceal­s the true nature of data collection or risky actions.
quote: Framing becomes unethical when it's used to mislead or conceal the truth

rule: Display privacy or safety scores prominently at decision points to incentivize good data practices and guide user choice.
quote: by making a privacy score front and center, users would be less likely to download apps with poor data practices

rule: Use recognizable familiar layouts to prepare the user's cognitive state and increase attentiveness to the message.
quote: I'm usually super attentive when looking at my notes. This ad puts my brain in that same state of mind as soon as it recognizes the layout

rule: Prioritize clarity and directness over clever creative; messages that are too clever risk unintended misinterpretation.
quote: If your message is too clever, some people will interpret it in ways you didn't intend, potentially resulting in a bad or deceptive experience

rule: Reorder workflow steps to place valued interactions earlier, increasing overall satisfaction.
quote: if you know customers love something at the end of their onboarding, try to shift this interaction to the beginning of the flow to increase overall satisfaction

rule: Show how user input shapes output immediately to honor the expectations created by personalization questions.
quote: Asking questions creates expectations. If you give your users the impression that you'll customize an experience based on their inputs, not delivering on that expectation can quickly backfire.

rule: Frame metrics and comparisons relative to user goals, not generic benchmarks.
quote: That way, the comparison is anchored to my goal (and not an unreachable amount of reading time every week)

rule: Auto-detect user device specifications and skip non-value steps; a 2% lift here compounds to hundreds of thousands of new users annually.
quote: A 2% lift at this first step could quickly compound to hundreds of thousands of new users per year.
finding: 20% of new visitors drop during download steps; auto-detection could recover 2% of those, scaling to hundreds of thousands annually

rule: Avoid sending notifications unrelated to user interests or follows; this triggers reactance and prompts users to disable all notifications permanently.
quote: Clubhouse is taking the liberty to send notifications that aren't related to the user's following or interests (which can trigger people to turn them off).
finding: 20+ notifications daily unrelated to user interests caused users to disable notifications entirely

rule: Use progress bars and streaks to leverage the Zeigarnik Effect; uncompleted tasks stay top-of-mind and guide user behavior.
quote: People remember uncompleted tasks better than completed tasks. A famous UX design example of this effect is the use of progress bars to guide a user's behavior.

rule: Request commitment (investment) immediately after reward moments; sunk-cost effect makes users value the product more and return sooner.
quote: Right after a reward is the best moment to ask your user to invest a bit of their resources in anticipation of future benefits.
finding: Investment wager step increased Day-7 retention by +14%

rule: Validate users' decisions before they act, especially on first actions, to build confidence and reduce friction.
quote: People seek validation to feel secure in their decisions - especially when it's the first time they take action.

rule: Limit survey response options; 11-point scales (0–10) add complexity without improving accuracy compared to simpler scales.
quote: NPS surveys impose 11 options (0 to 10), but research has shown that this extra complexity does not make the results more accurate
finding: Research shows 11-point scales do not improve accuracy over simpler options

rule: Avoid showing countdown timers with seconds unless deadline is under 60 seconds.
quote: avoid showing seconds unless the deadline is less than a minute away

rule: Be truthful about scarcity; trust determines how much scarcity pressure you can ethically apply.
quote: The amount of scarcity you can use is directly correlated to the amount of trust you've built

rule: Show adoption numbers to reduce social uncertainty; demonstrate others already use the product.
quote: Showing off the number of people who are already using it

rule: Show products in context or use cases to reduce social uncertainty among early adopters.
quote: Showing the product being used in context could help reduce social uncertainty

rule: Create information gaps to spark curiosity and motivate users to discover or engage with features.
quote: Your brain hates missing information. It creates a gap between what you know and what you want or need to know.

rule: Prioritize interface clarity and comfort when user reputation is tied to product experience, especially with personal content.
quote: If your product relies on virality, users will be more likely to share it if it makes them feel comfortable—especially when their face is next to the content.

rule: Never use asterisks with tiny text; it subconsciously triggers distrust by evoking decades of deceptive TV infomercial conditioning.
quote: decades of TV conditioned your brain to put the asterisk with the tiny text in the category of suspicious terms and conditions used when there's something to hide.

rule: Address users' primary pain point, not product features; address forgotten subscriptions in trial paywalls to increase signups by 23%.
quote: this simple demonstration of transparency led to a 23% lift in trial signups.
finding: 23% increase in trial signups

rule: Detect usage decline early; suggest new feature uses when you observe declining activity, not during cancellation.
quote: Start introducing new ways of using your product when you detect a decline in usage.

rule: Never mandate surveys in exit flows; mandatory but unnecessary steps create reactance and yield low-quality data.
quote: When mandatory but unnecessary steps block a natural flow, it creates reactance.

rule: Use real scarcity tied to actual resources and user benefits, not artificial countdowns; explain how sharing deliveries saves money.
quote: using a real limited resource (timing of deliveries), they are convincing new users to share the same restaurants as past users.

rule: Appeal to multiple senses in product presentation; mixing visuals, warmth hints, and scent cues increase engagement without feeling like marketing.
quote: We are engaged by things that appeal to multiple senses. The senses amplify one another when they are mixed.

rule: Minimize words and images in early onboarding; each element must earn its screen space with clear value for that moment.
quote: During the onboarding, users are immersed in a new world they don't know anything about, and that can be overwhelming. Each word/element should earn its place on the screen by adding clear value for this precise moment.

rule: Ask users about their goal or intent early and tailor subsequent steps; generic onboarding lifts activation by 10%.
quote: If you want successful users, you need to understand why they came to you. Generic goals won't cut it. Knowing the precise intent can generate a 10% activation lift.
finding: 10% activation lift

rule: Detect user intent from board names or inputs and proactively suggest premium features that match their likely use case.
quote: Detecting the most popular patterns in the board names and nudging their users to try some of their Power-Ups would boost their ratio of sign-up to PQL (Product Qualified Leads).

rule: Always surface a visible, discoverable back button or return path; loss of navigation causes anxiety.
quote: the #1 rule should always be to reassure people that they're at the right place and, if not, that they can easily find a way back

rule: Use a decoy option (slightly less attractive but relevant alternative) to make the primary choice easier by contrast.
quote: It's a lot easier to make a choice when we compare similar things. Our brain can quickly evaluate the differences

rule: Surface the customer's specific pain point (quota, usage limit) instead of exhaustive feature tables in checkout.
quote: Focus the journey of your customers around their most pressing pain point

rule: Remove header and footer navigation from critical conversion pages (signup, checkout); fewer links reduce abandonment.
quote: Removing your header & footer navigations in your most critical pages (e.g. signup, checkout) may lift your conversion rate by 28%
finding: 28% lift

rule: In multi-display or tall narrow layouts, move secondary navigation to the side edge and preserve vertical space for content.
quote: To make the most out of that width and preserve vertical space for content, controls that normally sit at the top and bottom, move to the side

rule: Use system navigation containers (NavigationStack, TabView, UINavigationController) instead of custom bars to opt into responsive layout behavior.
quote: make sure you're using the bars provided by navigation containers like TabView or NavigationStack

rule: In vertical bars, order items top-to-bottom: primary navigation (back/close) first, then prominent actions (done), then remaining items.
quote: Reserve the top for primary navigation controls, like back or close, followed by prominent actions, such as done

rule: Always provide both icon and title for toolbar items; let the system choose symbol-only or text+icon based on available space.
quote: Typically, your app specifies two pieces of data on your toolbar content, an icon and a title. Depending on the context and what's specified on the item, the system then chooses what representation to show

rule: Replace text+icon pairs with symbol+badge patterns to reduce vertical bar width and preserve space for more actions.
